idiom_name: abstract base class: public entry point + protected abstract hook
implementation_notes: TypeScript types the split: an abstract class cannot be instantiated, abstract members must be implemented by subclasses, and protected members are visible only to subclasses (the handbook documents both), so the public entry point plus protected abstract hook is the direct mapping of the classic structure. TS has no final, though - non-overridability is a declaration-level convention that the compiler enforces only for visibility, not against a derivative redefining the public method; noImplicitOverride plus an explicit override keyword makes every intended override visible in review, and the hook's signature and visibility are checked statically, which is strictly more than plain JavaScript offers.
pitfalls: protected and private are erased at compile time: after compilation the hook is an ordinary prototype property that JS consumers (or `as any`) can call or replace.
A derived class may still declare a public method with the same name as the wrapper - TypeScript accepts the override; only review or a lint rule (noImplicitOverride) surfaces it.
An abstract hook cannot have a default body, so a hook that needs a fallback must be a non-abstract protected method - then subclasses are not forced to provide it.
